title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education AI and Reading Comprehension Part 1
author: Shanahan, Timothy
summary: Shanahan responds to a teacher's question about whether AI-use policies allowing AI to translate, simplify, summarise, or synthesise texts undermine reading comprehension development. His answer is yes: because reading comprehension is fundamentally the ability to actively negotiate the affordances and barriers of text, having AI do that negotiation for students is like hiring someone else to do your exercise. The article focuses on AI text simplification, reviewing research showing AI can lower readability scores without improving comprehension -- and may reduce it by removing the difficulty that creates learning opportunity. Shanahan demonstrates this with a side-by-side of a Little House on the Prairie passage and its ChatGPT simplification: the revision loses information, emotional register, and cognitive challenge. His core argument: textual difficulty is not a bug to engineer away but the essential mechanism through which comprehension skill grows. Part 2 will address how AI could helpfully support literacy instruction.
points: - Reading comprehension is active and effortful: whoever negotiates the affordances and barriers of text gets the practice -- so AI doing it for students is cognitively inert for learners. - Research on AI text simplification shows it can lower readability scores without improving comprehension, and may introduce inaccuracies -- the Little House revision dropped emotional content and imagery the original contained. - Students make greater reading gains from grappling with texts they cannot yet read well than from texts matched to their current level -- challenge is the mechanism of growth, not a problem to remove. - Readability metrics are poor guides to text revision: adjusting sentence length and vocabulary rarely changes whether students comprehend content, and can produce texts that score easier but communicate less. - AI summarising or synthesising texts for students bypasses exactly the inferential, comparative, and integrative work that builds the comprehension capacity those tasks are meant to develop.
quotes: It makes sense to start with my definition of reading comprehension. It is the ability to make sense of information conveyed in written language -- the ability to negotiate the affordances and barriers of text. This is an active reader kind of definition. It includes understanding, inferring, judging, interpreting, relating, and remembering.

I find exercise to be tiring, sweaty, and often boring. I have often fantasized about hiring someone to do those things for me. Cyndie, my wife, is a bit of a killjoy. She is steadfast in her belief that I will have to do my own exercise if I am to benefit.
It is the same when it comes to learning to read. No one else can do that for you -- not even machines that have consumed hundreds of billions of words.

Despite their value for predicting how well kids will comprehend text, readability schemes have been lousy guides for text revision. The issue is whether shortening a few sentences and swapping out some vocabulary improves anybody's comprehension. Over the years, studies have usually said, no.
The revised sentence seems easier. But it fails to convey the same information, a problem that has plagued some efforts to use AI to produce readable health documents.

The revision might be easier for kids to understand. But avoiding those challenges has no possibility of helping students to become better comprehenders. The original text is the one that offers a possibility for teaching reading comprehension.

Using AI to revise or produce texts of certain levels of difficulty or using it to summarize and explain texts are ways teachers can avoid teaching reading comprehension, not scaffolds likely to make kids into better readers.
